slides.texte_overlay:
How to make people respect you
without raising your voice
Say what you mean in fewer words. Long explanations sound like apologies. "I can't do Saturday" is far stronger than five minutes of reasons and excuses nobody asked for.
Hold eye contact a second longer. When you make a point, don't look away straight after. A steady, calm look tells people you stand behind what you just said.
Name the problem, not the person. "The dishes keep piling up" works better than "You never clean." People respect the guy who solves problems without attacking anyone.
Be consistent. Same rules on Monday and Friday, same tone with your boss and your friends. People respect what they can predict, and they test what they can't.
Before: losing every argument because I got flustered. After: five minutes a day of history, art or science, and a calmer, clearer head when things get tense.
slides.texte_sophia: Before: losing every argument because I got flustered. After: five minutes a day on a micro-learning app like the Sophia app. A calmer, clearer head when things get tense.

slides.texte_overlay: Keep small promises. If you said you'd call back at five, call at five. Respect is built in tiny moments of reliability, long before any big moment arrives.
Walk away from disrespect calmly. "I'm not going to continue this if we're shouting." Then leave. Calmly refusing to play the game earns more respect than winning it.
